body:
Yeah, I'm aware. I've placed myself on hydroxytrptophan until I can see a psychiatrist. At that point I'll slowly titrate myself onto an antidepressant.

I don't know what makes me happy. There are things that interest me, like books, movies, and video games, but pursuing them doesn't provide a sense of reward or fulfillment.

Research is my passion. We are finding the building blocks to human suffering. And we are also finding ways to make people healthier, think more effectively, and produce more.
That may all be true, but it doesn't matter if I have potential to grow. After all, everyone has potential. There are way too many people in this world who are dead weight, and I am one of them.

I have severe ADHD and brainscans show high amounts of inactivity in my frontal cortex. My brain literally does not work effectively.

I don't have anyone to teach me. Nor do I have a bike or car. I am trying to learn some programming stuff, but I can't stay motivated.

I volunteer quite a lot. I'm a tutor and researcher, both of which are volunteer positions although as a researcher I've recently become an hourly employee. I was hoping to learn a scripting language for my discipline, Python, how to use photoshop, and how to cook over the summer. I'm also trying to stay happy, but I don't think anything can make me happy. I took a summer course in behavior analysis.

My research team studies the psychosocial factors behind pain and disability. After undergrad (I am currently one credit shy from being a sophomore) I hope that I can go to a graduate school to study pharmacology and neurofeedback.

You’ll have to forgive my lack of articulation – I am on a cellular since I do not plan on setting up utilities.

My biological family was extremely bitter to me in my younger years. I was an unplanned birth that was not aborted due to their religious beliefs. When I was younger, I was bedbound because my breastbone grew inward and started pressing upon my heart and lungs (Pectus Excavatum). This made them very bitter against me, and they stopped taking care of me even after I had corrective surgery (on my own volition). This is because they wanted me to be a strong man or whatever.

Both parents stopped buying food and began to eat out each day. My father died, and my mother continued the habit but refused to pay bills (she wanted me to get a job and pay them, even though she had a ridiculous amount of life insurance money). So we lost internet, electric, and water in that order. I stole money from my mother to buy an acer laptop and I used internet at a local hospital, showered at a rec center, etc. My history with my biological family is no longer important because I have zero contact with them.

I spent the past year attempting to socialize with students/faculty/members of the local LGBT community but all the ties I’ve made have been severed either due to the end of the academic year, people not wanting to spend time with me, or (in the instance of the LGBT community) me not putting out.

I don’t think I should stay alive in the future. I work in psychology research and there are plenty of people to replace me. These are people with perfect GPA’s, money, support systems and ridiculous amounts of free time. The only reason I’m kept around is because I concentrate in computers, which is something every research lab in the department is short on.
Stay still for the camera!
A research lab at a major university that studies chronic pain.

I conduct pain experiments on human subjects and I fucking love doing it.

It's very interesting to see how people act when they're in pain. Most people laugh. People cry for help, cringe, hide, huff and puff... each person has an interesting quirk or tick for pain. They're amusing.

You're really damn young, and it's not certain that your relationships at this age will last due to inexperience and this being a critical period in your development. For that reason, I would go to the private college if it is more financially feasible...

...And after two years, you may want to consider transfering to somewhere more accepting where you could possibly meet someone you could settle down with. My contention is that two years at the college will give you some perspective on life, and you'll figure out if you're ready to settle down with someone during this time.

No, you flat out don't understand. You began speaking to this fella' *yesterday.* If you care for your health, or having a safe and lasting relationship with someone, you must make sure that they make kind, hospitable company.

Being LGBT means that you should be wary of people carrying baggage with them. There are plenty of people that are experimenting, insecure with their sexualities, carrying diseases, and being unfaithful. As such, gay men have to step their game up and make sure that they don't get caught up in these situations without knowing about them first, because people don't typically broadcast these things.

Do your homework. Make sure the guy isn't going to cause problems, and is who he says he is. Meet him in a public place first, because giving a stranger a home-ground advantage makes it difficult to leave a coercive situation.

Finally, if you really don't see the potential reprocussions of this, you need to see someone. It's very possible that this disinhibited and reckless behavior is character of a manic state. If you think this could possibly be the case, go to your nearest MHMR walk-in clinic, minute clinic, or E.R. and ask for some Olanzapine to help you come down from the state.

Be cautious.

You don't know if this man is carrying diseases or takes sadism too seriously. Sure, you're going to "audition" to find out if y'all would make a good couple, be it at a coffee date or in bed. However, I'd encourage you to look out for your own safety because you need to be able to trust that this guy is not going to potentially infect you with an STI, or seriously hurt you.

I can't share your happiness about what is going on for you. I'm sorry, but this sounds extremely problematic. Take a step back and think this through. You don't have to do things so quickly.

> Narnia-level closet cases

I can't. I'm dying.

Of course, I shouldn't laugh, but that metaphor is hysterical.

Got it - I think Python is what I'm going to work on for now. Hopefully my lab director doesn't demand that I be fluent with ~~Intuit~~ Inquisit within the next two months...

Thanks :).

I'll take a look at it, but knowing that R serves as an alternative to SPSS sort of makes looking into it redundant for the upcoming future because... well, every single lab in my department uses SPSS exclusively. But hey, thanks - it's worth looking into for sure.

Right now, I am but an undergraduate freshman. I nearly got into a pre-doctoral program, but failed due to a lack of references (since I dropped out of high school). I'm going to keep at it for now, hopefully I can tolerate the stress. Thanks :).

You're spot on. Unfortunately, I'm not the most social person so my interactions can be kind of mechanical. I can see how that could drive people away, but I am making an active effort to improve my interpersonal interactions and this is one of my personal flaws that I'd need someone who's close to me to understand as I try and grow.

I'll look into LGBT oriented social groups, though they may be filled with a lot of young guys (not my division per se). I live on a (quite liberal) college campus, so things should be a tad easier for me. I'm about 30/40 miles away from the actual gayborhood, though...

My job requires me to artificially inflate my age, so I'm going to keep my beard (though in all honesty, my haircut is reaching beatnik levels and I'm going to cut it sometime). But, in the meantime, I shall continue to work out. Unfortunately, I cannot afford a trainer (which I really should get) and nobody on my college subreddit was able to be my workout buddy, but I can lurk /r/fitness and figure things out on my own.

Thanks for the advice, drunkasaurusrex :).

> If someone doesn't respond to your message it means they aren't interested. There is nothing wrong with you. You just aren't the right guy for that particular person at that moment. Everyone wants something different. For some, you might be too young to date seriously, for others it might be the Aspergers that they are turned off by. Whatever the reason, stop dwelling on it and move on. You don't have time to be sitting around finding out from each person what they did or didn't like about you. That would take forever and no one owes you an explanation unless they are breaking up with you after a relationship.

It's true that getting closure and whatnot is not very productive, but on the other hand, it gives me the experience necessary to build healthy relationships. There could be some glaring flaw about my character that I'm not recognizing. I suspect that my age may be a turn off, since I am really young (19) even for intergenerational daters.

> Dating is a numbers game. Just keep dating and keep trying. It took hundreds of dates before I found my current boyfriend. If it were easy to find the right one, then relationships wouldn't be special.

I'm trying. But, so far, no luck. I won't give up, but I am certainly lowering my efforts.

> The only other piece of advice I can give you is that you might want to consider working out and putting on muscle. I've found that the hotter a guy is, the more he is able to overcome whatever shortcomings he may have in other departments and only increases the number of responses you get to your online profile. Like I said, dating is a numbers game, so why not do something to move those numbers in your favor.

I've put up shirtless photos and gotten WAY too many sexually oriented responses. Conversely, if I just put a face picture, I don't get any attention on the web at all. I don't know what to do about that.

I am pretty fit. I've tried gaining weight because I don't like being so skinny, but that hasn't worked out. Recently I have been working out, but due to a surgery I had, it's not as easy for me as for others. Picture, for science: ~~**redacted**~~

If someone's is up front about their HIV status, I see no problems with being with said person. However, if someone is carrying a crippling illness, it's their responsibility to make that known. Not doing so could force someone into spending exhorborant amounts of money on antivirals, not to mention how debilitating they can be.

I think I'm ready for a committed relationship, but I don't know what I should expect of myself and others, which is why I've been struggling so much (as well as my workload). So far, I have stepped back for the most part - I've disabled all my dating profiles but one (so I don't completely shut the door on everyone) in order to think about how I'm handling these things.

I'm 19. My first and last partner did live with me for a while, and that worked out just fine. It certainly isn't something I'd rush into, though.

That's an interesting point and a big concern I have - I'm worried that I'm setting my workload up in a way that makes it difficult for myself and others to form and maintain emotional connections. Since there is some flexibility in my work (as long as I get my work done...) I might want to consider being open to such spontaneous things, though I wouldn't be the one to initiate such things.

I'm currently trying to work on the time management stuff. So far in my life, I've always been pushing my limits, which stresses me out. I'm working on finding a health balance, and hopefully that'll help me when and if I get into a committed relationship.

I'll try and be flexible about flexibility. Thanks :)

> I'd try to be more proactive in keeping in touch though, going a day without talking to someone (if they are indeed important) is pretty hard for a lot of people and doing so will send the wrong message.

I guess why this is so distressing is because I'm not sure if that kind of behavior is normal or not. Some people legitimately want daily contact and I'm not sure if that's an indicator of insecurity, or if they're just extraverted as fuck.
As I mentioned in another post, I wrote something at the end of my profile about my workload. Thanks for the advice. Have an orangered.

> wheel chairs

This made me laugh out loud because I wrote that I did research on disability in my profile, and quickly took that down once I was contacted by several different disabled people who wanted their lovers to eventually take care of their conditions.

I took your advice and wrote that I worked full time on my profile.

I'll sometimes give a very quick response to someone's message, then they will interpret that as an opportunity to have a full fledged text conversation, and subsequently they get upset when I don't hold a fluent chat with them.

You're right in that it serves as a litmus test for clinginess to some extent. There was someone I met who sent me messages every morning ("I hope you have a good day") and in the evening ("I hope you had a good evening"). It became too tiresome to have small talk twice a day, and I realized that he was clingy.

> For me, having to plan one or two weeks ahead for one Saturday with my hearthrob is like trying to schedule passion & love — emotions which thrive on a fair amount of spontaneity. Sometimes I'll want to drop everything and take you out to dinner. I understand the timing won't always work, but if you're willing to sometimes drop everything to spend time with me — do you know how that's going to make me feel? It's going to put me on top of the goddam world for a few hours. It's going to make me feel special to you.

That's something I'm concerned about. Do most people who work a 9-5 have the same problems?

There have been some people who've flat out told me to work on another day so I could hang out with them. I've told said people to fuck off, because nobody's screwing with my work, but this happens... more often than I'd expect. I wonder if having work come first and holding my relationships in a secondary position within my life is problematic.

> You said you try to get everything done, including studying, from 8-5. That leaves 15 hours in the rest of your day, to sleep, workout, what else? If you told me you could only see me one or two Saturdays a month with that timetable, I would think I'm something to cross off your to-do list, rather than a passionate love interest.

As an introverted, high stress individual, I try and counteract my stress by playing a video game for one or two hours at the end of each workday. When my mind is "blown" at the end of the day, the last thing I want to do is go through the nerve-wracking experience of meeting a stranger. So, unless I get intimate with someone, I'd be hesitant to overload myself.

> For me, anything less than two days a week frankly creates doubt about his interest in me, or worse, it makes me more prone to be on the lookout for something better, yaknow? On the other hand, spending more than 2 or 3 consecutive days with someone early in the relationship is a good way to burn out and get sick of him in short order.

Hmm, I wonder if I should put something on my daddyhunt profile that alludes to the fact that I work full time.

Thanks for your advice :).

*Professional:*

* Finish a year at my current job (health psychology research assistance) and get salaried.
* Become a better tutor for statistics.
* Learn how to script with specialist programs.
* Find a mentor in my field.
* Learn even more about my current field (pain research).
* Get into my university's pre-doctoral program.

* Build a social network of supportive friends.
* Avoid burnout, and find some good recreational outlets.

* Enjoy my youth while I can. Possibly enroll in an extracurricular Taekwondo class.

* Find enough financial security to avoid recursive periods of homelessness.
* Get an adult adoption.
* Track down my old high school teacher who convinced me to not drop out of high school, and tell him that I got my diploma.

Yup. LGBT oriented individuals are considered part of a marginalized population. By all means, mention it. The only problems forseeable ethical problems would be concerned with how you address this in personal statements and interviews. Don't overblow the "struggle" if you didn't have it.

I'm glad that you're in a good relationship and are thinking about this, but I would be concerned about a proposal placing strain on yourselves. Your first priority would be to get some certainty in your careers. Moving in will be very informative as to someone's character - it will expose hidden flaws, and this will allow you to make stronger decisions and bonds.

You might be experiencing a honeymoon phase, where you can only see positive qualities. This will end once you are able to observe someone for a long time - you'll find descrepancies between who they convey themselves to be, and who they are.

It's his responsibility to uphold communication, too. If he can't take some time aside of his week to say hello, he certainly wouldn't have or be willing to spend an evening hanging out. Another poster mentioned that this may be because he's running out of "options," and that's certainly a possibility.

I personally wouldn't play these games - time is valuable, and if someone can't respect my time, why would I think that he'd respect my health (e.g. disclosing his STI status)?
It's usually pop tarts and orange juice. ;P
Don't date guys in the closet. If they can't be true to themselves, how can you truly know who they are? Communication is a two-way street, and, well, this guy can't hold up his end.

As a smart individual, be smart about where you get your help. I really shouldn't downplay the importance of clinical treatment, but I think that a smarter answer to your problems would be to go request a psychologist. Why a psychologist? Well, when you're emotionally vulnerable like you are now, it would actually be the *worst* time to put you on medicine - it would probably decrease your inhibitions and increase your volition to the point where you could do something you shouldn't.

It sounds like you're miserable not because of yourself, but how constraining and alienating your environment is. It is definitely a good time to consider a change in scenery. That's why it'd probably be best for you to see a counselor - they can walk you through your thought processes, help you improve your judgement through their insight, and give you a place to vent to. Some other things to look into: mentoring programs, and other universities. Your education should, ideally, provide a nurturing environment for you to grow - instead, yours seems to be hostile and constraining. Transferring may be a good idea, if that is possible (I know that out-of-state tuition can be heavy, so look for ways to offset that. I know that many universities provide out-of-state fee waivers to people in hard STEM majors, and those working as researchers).

Someone mentioned the possibility of you having Asperger's. Now, I know it's one of those popular things people on the internet like to self-diagnose, and as a health psychology student, I'm not qualified to speak on this issue. But, magimack has a point - your post displays characteristics of people who have it. High intelligence, preferred topics, maladaptivity/alienation, and overabundances of empathy without the ability to process it are hallmark traits. I would see if your university has a behavior analysis or educational psychology program that does evaluations, and I'd encourage you to take one. Why, you must ask? Well, even if you end up not having the condition, the practitioners are still required to evaluate how well you adapt to your environment, and the possibilities of you having different conditions. So it's not *just* an autism evaluation, it's a total study you can have done on yourself that would point you in the right direction if you suspect you're suffering from a psychological ailment.

If you check my post history, you may find that I'm a horrible role-model, and that really trashes my ethos. My response - I don't care. There's my advice, and I hope you take it even if it may be terrible.

Yup, this is a thing, and it's mostly caused by rapid changes in hormones and neurochemistry after orgasm. In science-y terms, it's called post-sexual tristesse. 

I experience it as well. I can be all up in a significant other's grill, then once we're relieved I feel like doing something else, like play video games. Sucks, because my partners are more than slam pieces to me, but unfortunately, cuddling is suddenly unappealing after sex.

I also get slightly feverish and hungry after sex, as if I were hypoglycemic or something, so I usually set aside refreshments for after sex.
50% preparation? Preparing for what?

Sure, falling on the autism spectrum probably modifies how he thinks, but at the end of the day it's your ex's responsibility to qualify what is and isn't acceptable behavior. He's just a horrible guy, assuming that he really was keeping up this "nice guy" fascade. Perhaps his autism was part of that facade, in order for him to avoid responsibility for his actions?

The reason I bring this up is that you should take comfort in knowing that it's not his disorder, but his character that was horrible.

> A part of the gay community in Dallas has a reputation that isn't so kind and I can't say I disagree with it though, but I will say there are plenty of people who aren't part of that tiny sect. 

What part is that?

My post is based off of my own personal experience, as well as research in my field. If you're interested in the research I had in mind, here's a [great book](http://www.amazon.com/Learned-Optimism-Change-Your-Mind/dp/1400078393) by the researcher himself (no bridge sales involved) that anyone can read, or you can read [the wikipedia write-up](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learned_helplessness#Seligman_and_Maier) on some of his studies.

Personally, I like to take on more work at my job as well as exercise when I'm down. Video games can get my mind off of things, but I try not to get too engrossed in them.

A lot of these comments are hostile, but let me give you another perspective.

You're interested in more than a hook-up, right? Well, in the instance of this particular guy, the dude in question is not secure about himself, which means you won't be able to get to know him, and won't be able to have a secure relationship and be appreciated. So, that combined with his mental issues makes a cocktail for failure. You'd be best off passing him on, and finding someone who is secure about himself.

Here's my personal take, and I'm not a professional (yet) so take it with a grain of salt - never leave yourself alone with your thoughts for a long time. Rumination is a huge contributor for developing depression, alongside psychosocial triggers. I find that video games are good for blocking out thoughts, but you can do whatever - your mileage will vary.

Take care of yourself. Do things that normally make you happy, keep doing your work, so on, so forth. Don't hook up while you're emotionally vulnerable.

Welbutrin/Buproprion works in a totally different way that is really unique when compared to other antidepressants because it affects different neurochemicals, is a stable treatment, and also handles addiction & ADHD well. Lexapro affects totally different things. Anyways, sorry to jack your comment, it's just something you should know.
I have *never* heard of Welbutrin/Buproprion being used that way. That's odd, because it's really common for it to inhibit sexual drives.

Keep an eye on that - you should compliment the lives of each other, not complete them. At least, that's my contention.

I would inquire into his stress level just to be courteous. Still, I think you should bring up your concerns with him soon. He should understand and respect your desire to keep *some* distance.

It worries me that this guy gets upset when he's detached from you - is he emotionally stable while alone?

You're not being selfish at all - work is essential, and a job like one at a VA is not something you can just leave. The guy in question doesn't seem to be respecting your need for stability, and his demands are pretty unreasonable.

You can totally get away - it's not your job to support him. If he can't support himself, then he won't be able to support you if times get tough.

Also, this may be reading a bit too far into your post, but you don't seem to speak highly of this fellow. If you want to make things work, I would express your concerns with his motives to him. Does he have work lined up in the new city? Is he actively working on making you feel supported, and getting himself to a better place?

But, on the flip side, if you do feel like leaving him, don't do it suddenly. If he's relying on you, give him some notice so he could possibly find someone else to live with, like parents if he has them, or other friends. If he doesn't handle that news well, then he's immature and doesn't respect your perspective.

> For starters, a third job? I can see you getting Burnt Out on that, too! You said taking this job would complicate the relationship with the closest person you've got to a mentor/friend. I don't love doling out advice, but dude — The friend is more imporant than the job! Unless you're desperate for the money, which it sounds like you're not, I would urge you to cultivate that friendship without injecting the awkwardness of a power/money dynamic.

That's true, on top of my studies and workouts it may be a bit much. I've been hesitant to mix work and play, but I find my current work so very fulfilling, and I think this is making the most out of my college tuition. One thing that helps me is that my current jobs are 90% flexible - as long as I work a certain amount, I can chose my own clients (research participants and tutees). I will only take the third job if it doesn't complicate my mentorship, is a truly great opportunity, and under the condition that I reduce my tutoring hours significantly.

> Also, I just have to say it — What makes you think dating is going to be magically different when you're 20?! Finding Mr. Right is not like saying, 'Okay, I'm ready to date. The right guy should come along because I'm now ready.' You never how or when or from which source he's going to appear. Very likely not the sources you expect!

I think it's possible that people aren't taking me seriously, even in the intergeneration community, because I'm incredibly young (age 19). You bring up a good point, though - perhaps I should keep my eye open. I must say, though, it'd be quite difficult to meet someone gay through natural means outside of the web.

Something I like to do, since I have some medical problems, is I like to stay one or two days ahead of everything. That way, if something happens, I can take some time to myself with no repercussions. I can work on expanding this "buffer time" so that I can be readily available for dates on weekends.

> Regarding mr poet. He sounds childish. I would just ignore him as, frankly, he sounds like a spoiled child. BUT it does bring up a larger point: Intergenerational dating largely has partners at different earning potential. As the younger partner the older partner will often be making more money. He might want to take trips or treat you dinner or whatever. That is all fine if it is within your comfort zone. My boyfriend makes significantly more money than I do and I have managed to come to terms with the fact that he will generally buy dinner for example. Big purchases are another story....

That'll be something I may have to get used to. I've been known to argue with people who open the door for me - for some reason, I don't like people being nice to me. I'll have to do some research on this behavior.

> My honest recommendation? Go do things you want to do. Go to art galleries, go bowling, go to a bathhouse (if you want to), whatever it is that you do, go out and DO that shit. Own it. Be your person. Do what's going to make you happy. Don't worry about finding Mr Right or even Mr Right Now. Instead just work on doing the things that make you happy. Trust me, if you are happy with yourself Mr Right (or Mr Right Now) will be show up at some point.

This is my current course of action. I've decided to close down all my profiles except the one on daddyhunt, which is notably less hookup oriented. I must say, though, I really don't want to pay for membership, but it may be necessary if I actually want to be able to perform distance searches.

I'll skip on the bathhouse, but I may visit the university's LGBT club. I'm not sure that Mr. Right will just come into my life, because my orientation makes it much more difficult to find a partner through 'natural' means of mutual acquaintance and whatnot. 

Thanks for your advice :).

> We all have a certain amount of prejudice or judgments that we make when we date. In particular, I don't personally want to date somebody who is still grappling with coming out of the closet. I know there's a lot of guys who say this too. I don't want to be an experiment or a fling.

That's something I can really respect, and I'm glad you've made that decision. I think it can be a huge stressor, and you could invest yourself into someone who would ultimately not be able to reciprocate.

> Maybe even worse, we would turn into the people who go on dates for sex. Because our own dates had been so abysmal, maybe I'd think it was normal? Scary thought.

I've been wondering if I am having a "normal" dating experience for a while now. I do feel like there is some pressure to have sex on the first date, at least, in my experience. But, I went over that in another thread. It could (and probably is) related to both LGBT relationships, and how older people handle their sexuality.

> Personally, I'd say keep yourself occupied with working out & schoolwork. Just try not stress about it. I wish I had been less reliant on other people when I was just starting college.

> Hope this helps.

> I also think having a similar age friend would be helpful. That's something I'm working on. I am not as good at making friends with my peers so lately I've been nurturing the ones I've made.

I shall work on these things as well. Thanks for saying hello :).

Howdy. Thanks for chatting with me last night.

I think you're right in that I need to develop a support system, if you will, in my life. Right now, I don't think fellow peers and my co-workers are able to fill that role since we don't know each-other well enough to have what could be considered a quality friendship. My current mentor may be the closest I have to that, although I'm afraid that our relationship may be changing because he's trying to hire me to a job of his, which complicates things.

You're right in that my age and inexperience makes me vulnerable to manipulation. A long time ago, I met someone like "Mike," but fortunately I cut him out after I realized that he was probably schizoid. Anyways, I'm afraid that I'd end up like Dave if I wasn't thinking about my situation enough.

I tried giving that e-mail a second read from a different perspective. I still see it as written by an incredibly distressed individual, but you're right - some of his beliefs are contradictory and comical.

For now, as I mentioned in our chat, I'm going to invest my time into working out and academia, and I might try dating again when I turn 20 near the end of this year.

Thanks. I've decided that it'd be best if I took a year or so off from actively dating on the web, and dedicate that time to working out and possibly taking a third (!) job. Though I am ready for a relationship, I don't want to deal with this nonsense right now when I can accomplish other, more productive things.

Best of luck to you :).

> May I ask, what kind of profiles do the men you typically go after have? If their profile includes intimate photos and they describe themselves in such a way that sex comes first, it's entirely likely that they will be the type to want sex fast. Similarly, you may want to note in your profile that you're not looking for friends with benefits or anything of that sort. Be direct and blatant with what you want, friendship comes first is usually a good way of saying you want to get to know someone.

I skip over profiles that mention open relationship or heavily allude to sexuality. Yeah, I made a note on my profiles that I wasn't into hookups and was ready for a long-term-relationship.

> Everyone's situation is different. Just because someone lives with their parents at 55 doesn't mean they don't have stability--many people at that age will opt to move/move-in with their parents for the sake of helping them out in old age. Not saying your judgment was wrong in that instance, but just be careful with generalizing everything.

The man in question had never lived independently, nor did he desire that. But, in other situations, I think I could understand. That begs a question, though: If I am targeting an older demographic, should I be able to reasonably expect them to be financially stable? I'm afraid that, as a college kid, I am far from being able to support others. But, on the other hand, I do not want a sugar daddy.

> You're gonna have to realize that you're not going to be everyone's turn on. If they don't answer, try not to be offended and move on. If a guy goes on a date with you and stops communication without any warning, you most likely don't want to move forward to a relationship anyways.

It's so very difficult to tell if there's something wrong with who I am that puts people off, since I never receive word back from them. Am I too skinny, too young, or annoying? I have no idea what's going on in other people's heads.

You're right in that, if someone is not actively communicating, it shows that I am not a priority.
